body:
Eastern and western coastal plains of India

India's mainland coast borders the Arabian Sea in the west and the Bay of Bengal in the east. Differences in geological history, river systems, sediment supply and marine processes have produced contrasting coastal landscapes.

CharacteristicWestern coastEastern coast
Adjoining seaArabian SeaBay of Bengal
Coastal plainGenerally narrowerGenerally broader
Typical featuresEstuaries, rocky stretches, beaches and creeksExtensive deltas, coastal plains, beaches and lagoons
Major river-mouth examplesNarmada and Tapi estuariesMahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri deltas

The western coastal plain is relatively narrow along much of the Western Ghats. The eastward slope of much of the Peninsular Plateau directs several large river systems towards the Bay of Bengal, where they have built extensive depositional plains.

The western coastal plain is commonly described as a submerged coastal plain in Indian physiography, while the eastern coastal plain is generally described as an emergent coastal plain. These descriptions concern their broad geological development and do not imply that every local coastal segment has the same landforms or present-day direction of shoreline movement.

Important Indian coastal lagoons

  • Chilika Lake: Odisha, along the Bay of Bengal coast and south of the Mahanadi Delta. A sandy barrier separates much of the lagoon from the open sea.
  • Pulicat Lake: Shared by Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. The Sriharikota barrier separates the lagoon from the Bay of Bengal.

The Gujarat coastal landscape

Gujarat has a highly varied coast along the Arabian Sea. It can be broadly divided into 5 geomorphic regions:

  1. The Rann of Kachchh.
  2. The Gulf of Kachchh.
  3. The Saurashtra coast.
  4. The Gulf of Khambhat.
  5. The south Gujarat coast.

Gulf of Kachchh

Tidal processes are particularly important in the Gulf of Kachchh. Its coastal landscape includes mudflats, salt marshes, mangroves and coral reefs. Fine sediment accumulates in suitable sheltered and intertidal environments.

Gulf of Khambhat

The Gulf of Khambhat is characterised by a large tidal range and strong tidal currents. Its principal coastal features include extensive mudflats, creeks, estuaries and salt marshes.

The Narmada, Tapi, Mahi and Sabarmati drain into the Gulf of Khambhat. The Narmada and Tapi are particularly important examples of west-flowing Peninsular rivers that reach the sea through estuaries rather than extensive deltas.

Saurashtra coast

Wave action is especially important along exposed stretches of the Saurashtra coast. The region contains rocky shores, coastal cliffs, rocky terraces and sandy beaches. It demonstrates how erosional and depositional features can occur within the same coastal region.

South Gujarat coast and the Rann of Kachchh

Estuaries, creeks, marshes and mudflats are prominent along parts of the south Gujarat coast. The low-lying Rann of Kachchh contains extensive saline flats and seasonally inundated areas.

A tidal mudflat is a low-lying accumulation of fine sediment that is periodically submerged and exposed by tides.

The area between the ordinary high-water and low-water limits is called the intertidal zone. Mudflats are characteristic of sheltered environments in which fine sediments can accumulate.

The Gujarat coast cannot be classified entirely as erosional or depositional. Exposed rocky sectors, tide-dominated gulfs and sedimentary river mouths experience different combinations of coastal processes.

Prelims focus

  • Narmada and Tapi are associated with estuaries on the western coast.
  • Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri form major eastern coastal deltas.
  • Chilika is in Odisha; Pulicat is shared by Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
  • Narmada, Tapi, Mahi and Sabarmati drain into the Gulf of Khambhat.
  • The Gulfs of Kachchh and Khambhat are strongly influenced by tides.
  • Trap: Beaches and depositional landforms also occur on India's western coast.

[References: NCERT, Class 9, Contemporary India-I, Chapter 2, The Coastal Plains, 2025-26 reprint, p. 13; NCERT, Class 11, India Physical Environment, Chapters 2-3, Coastal Plains and Peninsular Drainage sections; National Centre for Coastal Research, National Assessment of Shoreline Changes along Indian Coast, July 2018, Section 4.3.1, p. 19, historical assessment for 1990-2016; Andhra Pradesh Government, Tirupati District, Pulicat Lake; Space Applications Centre, National Wetland Inventory and Assessment, Andhra Pradesh, Section 9.4. Online sources consulted on 28 November 2026.]

title: Coastal Landforms of India and Gujarat

body:
The changing position of a shoreline

The shoreline is the line at which land and water meet at a given time or specified water level. Its position changes over short periods because of tides, waves and storms, and over longer periods because of sediment movement and changes in sea level and land elevation.

Long-term shoreline change is commonly described using 3 conditions:

  • Erosion or retreat: The shoreline moves landward as coastal material is lost.
  • Accretion or advance: The shoreline extends seaward through sediment accumulation.
  • Relative stability: The shoreline experiences little net movement over the period considered.

A temporarily stable shoreline is not necessarily inactive. Sediment can continue moving into and out of the area without causing substantial long-term displacement.

Coastal sediment budget

A sediment budget describes the balance between the sediment entering and leaving a coastal area.

Rivers, eroding cliffs and neighbouring shores can supply sediment. Waves, coastal currents and movement into deeper water can remove or redistribute it.

  • When sediment supply exceeds sediment removal, the coast tends towards accretion.
  • When sediment removal exceeds sediment supply, the coast tends towards erosion.
  • When the two are approximately balanced over time, the coast may remain relatively stable.

The sediment budget is particularly useful for understanding sandy and muddy coastlines. Sea-level changes and wave energy also influence how a shoreline responds.

Relative sea-level change

Relative sea level is the height of the sea surface in relation to the adjoining land. It can change because the ocean surface moves, the land moves vertically, or both occur together.

Eustatic and land-level changes

ChangeMeaningLikely relative effect
Eustatic sea-level riseRise in global mean sea levelFavours coastal submergence
Eustatic sea-level fallFall in global mean sea levelFavours coastal emergence
Land upliftLand surface risesRelative sea level falls if sea surface is unchanged
Land subsidenceLand surface sinksRelative sea level rises if sea surface is unchanged

Global sea-level rise can result from thermal expansion of warming seawater and the addition of water from melting land-based glaciers and ice sheets.

Land uplift and subsidence can result from geological processes. Subsidence may also be accelerated by sediment compaction and excessive groundwater extraction.

Emergent and submerged coasts

An emergent coast develops when relative sea level falls and previously submerged coastal surfaces become exposed. Raised beaches and elevated former marine terraces may indicate emergence.

A submerged coast develops when relative sea level rises and seawater occupies previously exposed land. Flooded river valleys and other drowned coastal features may indicate submergence.

Shoreline accretion and coastal emergence are not identical. Accretion results from sediment accumulation, whereas emergence concerns a fall in relative sea level. Similarly, a coast may retreat through erosion without any rise in relative sea level.

Human influences on shoreline change

  • River dams: May reduce the delivery of sediment to downstream beaches and deltas.
  • Sand mining: Can remove sediment that would otherwise support beaches and coastal barriers.
  • Groynes: Structures extending across the shore that interrupt longshore sediment transport. Accumulation on the sediment-receiving side may be accompanied by increased erosion farther along the coast.
  • Seawalls: Structures intended to protect coastal land from direct wave action. They may protect local property while causing or intensifying beach loss under some conditions.
  • Removal of dunes and mangroves: Can reduce natural coastal protection and sediment stability.

Prelims focus

  • Accretion is the net accumulation of coastal sediment.
  • A negative sediment budget generally favours erosion.
  • Land subsidence increases relative sea level when other conditions remain unchanged.
  • Raised beaches can indicate coastal emergence.
  • Groynes interrupt longshore sediment transport.
  • Trap: Landward shoreline retreat does not necessarily prove that global sea level has risen.

[References: US Geological Survey, An Overview of Coastal Land Loss, Open File Report 03-337, Physical Agents of Land Loss: Sediment Budget and Rivers and Deltas; IPCC, Climate Change 2022: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability, Chapter 3, Section 3.2.2.2; NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Landforms and their Evolution, Waves and Currents section; Newcastle University, Co-Curate, Longshore Drift. Online sources consulted on 28 November 2026.]

body:
Landforms and landscapes

A landform is an individual natural physical feature of the Earth's surface, such as a hill, valley, beach or sea cliff. A landscape consists of several associated landforms occupying a larger area.

Landscape evolution refers to the development and transformation of these features through time. It results from interactions between processes originating within the Earth and processes operating at or near its surface.

Endogenic and exogenic processes

CharacteristicEndogenic processesExogenic processes
Principal originEarth's internal energySurface energy, gravity and climatic influences
ExamplesUplift, folding, faulting, volcanismWeathering, mass wasting, erosion and deposition
Typical influenceCreates or modifies elevation and reliefWears down, redistributes and deposits surface material

Relief is the difference in elevation between higher and lower parts of a landscape.

Endogenic processes frequently create new relief through uplift and deformation. Exogenic processes then modify this relief by breaking down rocks, moving material and depositing it elsewhere.

However, the distinction is not simply that internal processes always build land and external processes always destroy it. Tectonic subsidence can lower land, while deposition can construct plains, deltas and beaches.

Weathering, mass wasting, erosion and deposition

  • Weathering: Breakdown or alteration of rock in its original position without requiring transportation of the resulting material.
  • Mass wasting: Downslope movement of rock, soil or debris directly under the influence of gravity.
  • Erosion: Removal of material by moving agents such as rivers, wind, glaciers and waves.
  • Deposition: Accumulation of transported material where movement or transporting capacity decreases.

Weathering, mass wasting, erosion and transportation contribute to the wearing down of the land surface, collectively described as denudation.

Controls on landscape evolution

Geological structure and rock resistance

Rock composition, hardness, permeability, bedding, joints and faults influence how rapidly a landscape is modified. Less resistant rocks generally erode faster than more resistant rocks under comparable conditions.

Tectonic activity

Uplift increases land elevation and may steepen river gradients. Faulting can create steep slopes, depressions and structural weaknesses. Subsidence can produce basins in which sediments accumulate.

Climate

Temperature and precipitation strongly influence weathering, vegetation, runoff and slope stability. Warm and humid conditions often favour chemical weathering, while repeated freezing and thawing can promote mechanical breakdown where suitable conditions occur.

Time

The appearance of a landscape reflects the cumulative effects of processes operating over different periods. Some changes occur slowly over geological time, whereas earthquakes, floods, storms and landslides may modify landforms rapidly.

Interaction between tectonics and climate

Tectonic uplift and climate act together rather than independently. When mountains are uplifted, the newly created slopes and relief may increase the potential for river incision and gravity-driven slope movement.

Where moist winds are forced to rise over mountain barriers, cooling and condensation can produce orographic rainfall. Increased precipitation may then increase runoff, chemical weathering and erosion.

Rivers transport sediment eroded from uplands into valleys, plains and coastal areas. Consequently, tectonic and climatic conditions far inland can influence the development of deltas and beaches.

The Himalayas illustrate this interaction: tectonic mountain building creates high relief, while rivers, glaciers, rainfall and mass movements modify the mountains and transfer sediment towards adjoining plains and river mouths.

Prelims focus

  • Uplift, folding and faulting are endogenic processes.
  • Weathering does not require transportation.
  • Mass wasting is driven directly by gravity.
  • Climate influences the intensity and type of weathering and erosion.
  • Tectonic uplift can renew the potential for erosion.
  • Trap: Exogenic processes also build landforms through deposition.

[References: NCERT, Class 7, Our Environment, 2018-19 edition, Chapter 3, pp. 12 and 15-16; NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Geomorphic Processes, and Landforms and their Evolution, SATHEE online editions; NCERT, Class 11, India Physical Environment, Structure and Physiography section. Online sources consulted on 28 November 2026.]
